601.event_title: The Merovingian 'do-nothing kings' fade before the mayors of the palace
601.place: Frankish kingdom (now France, Belgium and western Germany)
601.event: After King Dagobert I died in 639, the later Merovingian kings of the Franks came to be called rois faineants, do-nothing kings, because real authority passed step by step to the mayors of the palace who governed in their name. By the 740s the mayors were placing Merovingians such as Childeric III on the throne only to keep up the appearance of royal rule. In 751 the mayor Pippin, with papal approval, had himself made king, and Childeric was deposed, tonsured and confined to the monastery of Sithiu near Saint-Omer.
601.explanation: The dynasty that had founded the Frankish kingdom did not fall in a single blow; its authority dimmed over about a century until it could be removed without a struggle.
601.tie_back: The kural pictures a family as a lamp that grows dim as the grime of sloth settles on it, and the Merovingian line faded in exactly this gradual way until its light went out.
601._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a lineage dimming gradually through inaction; historians note that many of these kings came to the throne as children, so their 'idleness' was partly powerlessness.

602.event_title: Fourteen-year-old Alfred Krupp takes on his father's failing works
602.event: When Friedrich Krupp died on 8 October 1826, he left his family a small, heavily indebted steel works in Essen where production had almost come to a standstill. His fourteen-year-old son Alfred, working alongside his widowed mother, took on the management of the workshop and its handful of employees. He became sole proprietor in 1848 and built the firm into one of the largest industrial enterprises in Europe.
602.explanation: The family's standing was saved not by inheritance, which was nearly worthless, but by years of relentless daily work by a teenage heir.
602.tie_back: The kural says those who want their family to be a family in the full sense must put laziness to death in their daily conduct, and young Alfred Krupp restored his family's fortunes through exactly that kind of unremitting work.
602._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of effort restoring a family's standing; the firm's later role as an arms maker is outside this example.

603.event_title: Ahmad Shah, the last Qajar shah, is deposed while living in Europe
603.event: Ahmad Shah, who had come to the throne of Iran as a boy in 1909, left for Europe in 1923 on a journey of indefinite length and never returned. While he was absent, Iran's national assembly, the Majles, formally deposed him in October 1925, ending the Qajar dynasty, and the crown was conferred on Reza Khan. Ahmad Shah settled permanently in France and died about four years later.
603.explanation: A ruling house that had governed Iran since the late eighteenth century came to an end while its last ruler, absent from his country, was still a young man.
603.tie_back: The kural says the family of one who clings to idleness dies before he does, and the Qajar dynasty ended while its absent shah lived on in exile.
603._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the dynasty's death before its last ruler matches the kural closely, but the sources document his prolonged absence and political weakness, not laziness as such, and larger political forces drove the change.

604.event_title: Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa withdraws into the arts as the Onin War begins
604.event: Ashikaga Yoshimasa became shogun in 1449 but proved an ineffective ruler, and the great lords increasingly ignored his orders. A succession dispute between his brother Yoshimi and his son Yoshihisa helped set off the Onin War of 1467-1477, which devastated Kyoto and left shogunal authority badly weakened. Yoshimasa devoted himself to the tea ceremony, painting and patronage of the arts, and in retirement built his villa at Higashiyama, later the temple Ginkakuji.
604.explanation: Yoshimasa's patronage shaped Japanese culture, but his neglect of government coincided with the collapse of his house's real power and the start of a century of civil war.
604.tie_back: The kural says that for those who sink into sloth and make no worthy effort the family collapses and faults multiply, and under Yoshimasa the Ashikaga shogunate declined while disorder spread across Japan.
604._accuracy_note: A strong fit for neglect leading to a house's decline and multiplying troubles, though Yoshimasa was active as an aesthete rather than simply idle, and the Onin War had deeper causes.

605.event_title: The Swiss watch industry is overtaken by the quartz watch
605.event: Although quartz timekeeping had been developed in Switzerland, Swiss watchmakers were slow to adopt it, while Seiko of Japan launched the Quartz Astron, the first quartz wristwatch on the market, on 25 December 1969. Cheaper and more accurate quartz watches from Asia then took over the market, and by the late 1970s the two largest Swiss watch groups were close to insolvency. Employment in the Swiss watch industry fell from almost 90,000 at the end of the 1960s to about 30,000 by the mid-1980s, before the Swatch, launched in 1983, helped lead a recovery.
605.explanation: A world-leading industry that delayed acting on a technology it had helped create lost most of its jobs within about fifteen years.
605.tie_back: The kural names delay and heedlessness among the pleasant vessels that carry people to ruin, and the Swiss watchmakers' slowness to act on quartz carried a proud industry close to collapse.
605._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of procrastination and complacency leading toward ruin; the kural's other two vices, sloth and oversleeping, are not part of this story, and recession also played a role.

606.event_title: Commodus inherits the Roman Empire from Marcus Aurelius
606.event: Commodus succeeded his father, Marcus Aurelius, in 180 at the height of the Roman Empire's power and wealth. He showed little interest in the work of government, leaving it to a series of favourites, and devoted himself to appearing in the arena as a gladiator and hunter of wild beasts. He was killed by conspirators from his own household on 31 December 192, and the empire soon fell into civil war.
606.explanation: Commodus received one of the greatest inheritances any ruler has known, yet his reign is remembered as the end of Rome's most stable era.
606.tie_back: The kural says that even if the idle inherit the wealth of world-ruling kings, they will rarely gain any real good from it, and Commodus came into the whole Roman world and gained nothing worthy from it.
606._accuracy_note: A strong fit for squandered inheritance through neglect of duty, though Commodus was energetic in his own pursuits rather than idle in the ordinary sense.

607.event_title: Lincoln rebukes General McClellan for his slowness and then removes him
607.place: Washington, D.C., and Maryland, United States
607.event: After the Battle of Antietam on 17 September 1862, General George McClellan did not pursue the retreating Confederate army for weeks despite President Lincoln's urging. When McClellan reported in October that his cavalry horses were sore-tongued and fatigued, Lincoln telegraphed back asking what the horses had done since Antietam that could have tired them. On 5 November 1862 Lincoln ordered him relieved of command and replaced by General Ambrose Burnside.
607.explanation: Repeated urging gave way to open sarcasm and finally to dismissal, and McClellan never received another military command.
607.tie_back: The kural says those who give themselves to idleness will hear sharp rebukes and then scornful words, and McClellan's inaction drew first Lincoln's prodding, then his cutting telegram, and then removal.
607._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of rebuke escalating to scorn; McClellan's slowness came from excessive caution rather than simple laziness.

608.event_title: King Charles IV of Spain gives up his crown to Napoleon at Bayonne
608.place: Madrid and Aranjuez, Spain, and Bayonne, France
608.event: Charles IV, king of Spain from 1788, lacked leadership qualities and from 1792 left the government largely to the royal favourite Manuel de Godoy, while he preferred hunting to governing. In March 1808 a riot at Aranjuez forced him to abdicate in favour of his son Ferdinand. Napoleon then summoned the royal family to Bayonne, where both father and son gave up the crown, which Napoleon gave to his brother Joseph, and Charles spent his remaining years in exile under French supervision.
608.explanation: The heir to one of Europe's oldest crowns ended as a pensioner of the foreign ruler whose armies had occupied his country.
608.tie_back: The kural warns that if sloth settles in a person of noble birth it will make him a subject of his enemies, and Charles IV's neglect of rule ended with his kingdom in Napoleon's hands and himself in Napoleon's custody.
608._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of high birth, indolence and subjection to an enemy, though Napoleon's ambitions would have threatened Spain under any king.

609.event_title: The idle young Charles Darwin becomes a dedicated naturalist
609.place: Shrewsbury, Edinburgh and Cambridge, England and Scotland, and the voyage of HMS Beagle
609.event: Darwin's father, a physician, regarded his teenage son as a wastrel interested mainly in shooting, and Darwin later recorded in his autobiography that his father once told him he cared for nothing but shooting, dogs and rat-catching and would be a disgrace to himself and his family. He abandoned medical studies at Edinburgh and was sent to Cambridge to prepare for the church, where he became a keen collector of beetles and a student of the botanist John Henslow. Through Henslow he joined HMS Beagle in 1831, and the five-year voyage turned him into a tireless naturalist whose work culminated in On the Origin of Species in 1859.
609.explanation: The young man his father feared would disgrace the family became its most celebrated member once he committed himself to sustained work.
609.tie_back: The kural says that when a person throws off the rule of sloth, the faults that had attached to his family and his own worth disappear, and Darwin's transformation turned a feared family disgrace into lasting honour.
609._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of turning from idleness to effort and redeeming a family's hopes; the young Darwin's pastimes were energetic sport rather than inactivity.

610.event_title: Alexander the Great's campaigns from Macedonia to India
610.place: From Macedonia across Asia Minor, Egypt and Persia to the Indus valley
610.event: Alexander, king of Macedon from 336 BCE, crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the Persians at the Granicus, at Issus in 333 BCE and decisively at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Marching almost continuously, he took Egypt and the Persian capitals and reached the Indus valley, where he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE. When his exhausted troops refused to go further east he turned back, and he died at Babylon in 323 BCE, ruler of an empire stretching from Greece to northwestern India.
610.explanation: In about eleven years of almost ceaseless campaigning, one king brought a greater share of the known world under his rule than anyone before him.
610.tie_back: The kural promises that a king free of sloth will gain all at once the whole world that Vishnu's strides covered, and Alexander's unresting campaigns are history's most famous example of a ruler winning a vast realm in a single lifetime.
610._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of tireless energy winning vast dominion; the kural praises diligence while Alexander's story is also one of war, and his empire divided soon after his death.
